newsitem.title: GERMANY: Serb charged in Germany with genocide in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Serb charged in Germany with genocide in Bosnia.

text.p: The German Federal Prosecutor's Office said on Tuesday it had charged a 49-year-old Serbian with genocide and murder for his role in the violent expulsion of Moslems from their homes during the Bosnian war.

The office said the man, identified only as Nikola J., was believed to have led a group of Serb fighters responsible for killing about two dozen Moslems in 1992 in the region around the town of Doboj.
The suspect, who was a member of the Serb Democratic Party (SDS) in Doboj, was detained in Duesseldorf on December 16, 1995, and has been in investigative custody since.

He is believed to have been one of two men who deliberately fired machineguns into a group of Moslems in the town of Grapska on June 14 or 15, 1992, killing 22 people, including three women and a child.
On June 19, the fighters arrested the entire Moslem population of the village of Sevarlije.

Prosecutors say Nikola J. picked out two of the Moslems and ordered one of his fighters to shoot one of them, which he did. The second Moslem was then killed in a flurry of shots fired either by the soldier or Nikola J.

In late September of the same year, he is accused of having placed a metal bucket over the head of a detainee in the central prison in the town of Doboj and then pounding the pail with a one-metre long (three-foot) wooden club. The victim died of his injuries.

Nikola J. is also accused of psychologically torturing Moslem prisoners. He is alleged to have placed a water bottle on the head of one Moslem and fired at it, telling the prisoner: "If I hit it, you're in luck. If I miss, you're out of luck."
In the town of Mala Bukovica, he is believed to have pointed his machine gun at two Moslem prisoners before firing narrowly past their heads at the last minute, and then robbing them of their money.

Tuesday's statement from the prosecutor's office said Nikola J. had been formally charged in Duesseldorf on September 11 with genocide in 14 cases, in combination with murder, causing grievous bodily harm, unlawful detention and blackmail with intent to rob.

Although the offences were not committed in Germany, Nikola J. can be tried here under a passage of international law which says that the perpetrators of genocide may not receive shelter anywhere and can be tried abroad.
Nikola J. lived in Germany from 1969 to 1992 and this is considered a sufficient link with the country for him to be tried here.

The case is not linked to the United Nations War Crimes Tribunal in The Hague. The tribunal has so far indicted over 70 Bosnian Serbs, Croats and Moslems, but only a few have been arrested while the majority are still at large.
